newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O.LICHT - Second world 96/97 sugar output estimate.
newsitem.headline: F.O.LICHT - Second world 96/97 sugar output estimate.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any enquiries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
SECOND ESTIMATE OF WORLD SUGAR PRODUCTION 1996/97
(First figure 1996/97, second figure 1995/96, figures in brackets previous estimate of October 10, 1996, all figures in 1000 tonnes, raw value.)
World sugar production 125304/123069 (126613)
World beet sugar production 37576/36416 (36417)
World cane sugar production 87728/86653 (90196)

World sugar production in 1996/97 is now forecast to amount to around 125 million tonnes. This is rather more than one million tonnes below the assessment we made in mid-October last year but it is still well in excess of consumption needs.

Consequently one can expect to see a further build up of stocks. In 1995/96 there was already a heavy weight of stocks overhanging the market but this did not result in any calamitous fall in prices. This led some to believe that the relationship between stocks and prices no longer holds good.

What happened last year, however, was that a substantial proportion of the surplus stocks were to be found in India and for political and infrastructural reasons only a small proportion of these could be made available for export. Circumstances are different this year. The surplus is likely to be more widely spread and consequently more easily made available for the market.

The autumn weather was very favourable to beet sugar production in Europe and output in the EU is now put at 17.8 million tonnes, raw value, up by 806,000 tonnes after 476,000 tonnes the previous season.

Output in those Western European countries outside the EU is also expected to be sharply higher. Among the East European countries Poland also has a larger crop this season, which may cause some internal problems, but the two large producers in the former Soviet Union, the Ukraine and Russia where a myriad problems prevail, will both have lower production than last season at 2.9 and 1.9 million tonnes respectively. At 3.6 million tonnes, the US will produce slightly more than last season while China's output from beet is estimated at 1.5 million tonnes.

In the years from 1987/88 to 1995/96 beet sugar production has fallen at an average annual rate of 0.7 per cent. In the much more dynamic cane sector, however, there has been an average annual growth of 3.5 per cent.

Further growth is expected in the cane sector in 1996/97 but there will be a setback in Asia where output in India is expected to drop by more than two million tonnes, though it will still amount to some 15.7 million tonnes, raw value, to make the country once again the world's highest producer.
Output in China is expected to rise from 5.4 to 5.7 million tonnes while Thailand is expected to reach another record with 6.4 million tonnes.
Despite official statements to the contrary, it seems likely that the Helms-Burton law will adversely affect Cuba's growth plans. We are anticipating a marginal increase to 4.7 million tonnes.

Around that total will also be produced by Mexico, which was more than originally forecast, whilst output in Guatemala continues to rise with rather more than 1.4 million tonnes expected in 1996/97. The giant in South America is Brazil which is expected to reach nearly 15 million tonnes.

South Africa will produce nearly 2.4 million tonnes this year. Though not quite up to earlier hopes it is a welcome recovery after four weather savaged crops in succession. Production continues to rise in Australia, where output in 1996/97 is put at 5.6 million tonnes.

Though world production will again exceed consumption so that stocks will rise once again, the rate of growth is falling. In part this reflects the drop in output in India but the world market price which is below production costs in most countries will also have had its effect. If there is no major price rise in 1997 - and certainly there is no reason to expect one - this may well have an effect on output in 1997/98.
